Field notes

Start with one useful thing

Your first app does not have to run your whole business. It needs to make one part of it easier.

Atomic · Product perspective · 3 min read

On this pageStart where the friction isMake the first version smallUse the app to learnBring that focus to Atomic

Start where the friction is

A studio owner answers the same scheduling questions every week. A small shop shares product details across a string of messages. A freelancer sends another email explaining where a project stands.

Each is a modest problem with a recognizable cost: time, attention, or uncertainty. Each is also a useful starting point for an app.

Make the first version small

It is tempting to add a dashboard, notifications, payments, and a loyalty program before anyone has tried the main workflow. But each addition introduces another decision and another way for the experience to become confusing.

For a booking app, the first useful version might let someone choose a service and request a time, then let the owner confirm it. That is enough to ask whether the app makes the exchange clearer.

Use the app to learn

Show the first version to someone who would use it. Ask them to complete the task without explaining every screen. Notice where they hesitate and which information they look for.

The next improvement may be a better label or a clearer confirmation, not a new feature. A narrow first version makes those observations easier to act on.

Bring that focus to Atomic

Atomic starts with a description of what you want to build. The more clearly you can explain the person, the task, and the result, the better a starting point you have for reviewing the app.

Think of your first brief as a hypothesis: this small piece of software will make this particular job easier. Build enough to try it, then decide what comes next.
